pages.text: The great war at Troy was over at last, and the hero Odysseus longed only for home. He was king of a small green island called Ithaca, where his wife Penelope and his young son waited for him. He gathered his men, boarded his ships, and set sail across the wide, dark sea. Home, he thought, could not be far.

image.note: Odysseus standing proud at the prow of his ship as it leaves a distant war-torn shore, men rowing, a single square sail full of wind; open sea ahead; determined and hopeful

pages.text: But the sea had other plans. A furious storm, sent by the god of the ocean himself, seized the ships and flung them far off course. Day after day they were driven across strange waters, past unknown shores. Odysseus gripped the mast and stared at the horizon. Getting home, he began to fear, would take all the cunning he had.

image.note: A small ship tossed on huge dark waves under a wild sky, sail straining, men clinging on; Odysseus gripping the mast, water flying; dramatic but not frightening

pages.text: They landed on an island to search for food and found a great cave stacked with cheeses. But the cave belonged to a Cyclops, a giant with a single eye in the middle of his forehead. He rolled a huge stone across the mouth of the cave, trapping the men inside, and grinned hungrily at the tiny figures below.

image.note: Inside a vast cave: a towering one-eyed giant rolling an enormous round stone across the entrance, tiny sailors huddled among giant cheeses and pails; dim, tense, cartoonish not gory

pages.text: Odysseus could not beat such a giant with strength, so he used his wits instead. "What is your name?" growled the Cyclops. "Nobody," said Odysseus. He gave the giant strong wine until he slept, then put out his one great eye. The Cyclops roared, "Nobody has hurt me!" so no one came to help. At dawn the men crept free beneath his woolly sheep.

image.note: Dawn at the cave mouth: sailors clinging cleverly to the undersides of large woolly sheep as they file past the groaning, blinded giant who feels only the sheeps' backs; comic cunning, no gore

pages.text: Next they came to the island of Aeolus, keeper of the winds. He welcomed them kindly and gave Odysseus a wondrous gift: a leather bag holding all the stormy winds, tied tight with a silver cord. "Keep it shut," he warned, "and only the gentle west wind will carry you home." For nine days they sailed, and Ithaca came into sight.

image.note: Aeolus handing Odysseus a fat leather bag bound with a silver cord on a bright windy island; the crew watching; friendly, generous mood

pages.text: But while Odysseus slept, his curious crew untied the bag, certain it was full of gold. Out howled every wind at once. The ships were snatched up and hurled all the way back across the sea, far from the home they had almost touched. Odysseus woke to find his island gone from view once more. He could have wept.

image.note: The leather bag bursting open on deck, a swirl of wild winds spiralling out, sailors thrown back in alarm, the sail whipping; Odysseus waking, dismayed; the green island shrinking far behind

pages.text: On the next island lived Circe, a powerful enchantress. When some of the crew knocked at her door, she smiled and offered them food, then waved her wand and turned them all into grunting pigs. Odysseus marched to her hall to save them, protected by a magic herb the god Hermes had secretly pressed into his hand.

image.note: Circe in a grand hall waving a wand, a cluster of startled pigs where sailors had stood; Odysseus striding in bravely, a small green herb in his fist; fairy-tale, not scary

pages.text: When Circe's spell would not work on him, she gasped in wonder and knew at once that this was the famous Odysseus. She changed his men back from pigs to sailors, and welcomed the weary travellers warmly. They rested on her island a while, and when at last they left, Circe warned Odysseus of the strange dangers still ahead.

image.note: Circe touching a pig which is transforming back into a grateful sailor; Odysseus watching, relieved; the hall now warm and welcoming; wonder on Circe's face

pages.text: The first danger was the Sirens, whose singing was so beautiful that sailors who heard it steered onto the rocks and were lost. Odysseus longed to hear the song and still live to tell of it, so he made a daring plan. He softened beeswax and pressed it into the ears of every man aboard, so not one of them could hear.

image.note: Sailors stopping their ears with beeswax as the ship approaches rocky islets where shadowy Siren figures sing; Odysseus giving orders; tense anticipation, the Sirens not gruesome

pages.text: Then he ordered the crew to tie him tightly to the mast and, whatever he did, never to free him until the danger had passed. The Sirens sang, and their song was lovelier than anything he had ever known. He begged and strained to be released, but his men rowed steadily on, and soon the deadly voices faded far behind.

image.note: Odysseus bound to the mast straining against the ropes, face full of longing, as deaf rowers pull steadily past the singing Sirens; the ship slipping safely by

pages.text: Ahead lay a narrow strait guarded by two terrors. On one side lurked Scylla, a snapping monster high in a cave. On the other churned Charybdis, a whirlpool that swallowed the whole sea and spat it back. To sail between them was to risk everything, and there was no other way home. Odysseus set his jaw and took the helm himself.

image.note: A narrow sea passage between towering cliffs: a shadowy many-headed monster in a high cave on one side, a vast swirling whirlpool on the other, the tiny ship threading between; Odysseus firm at the helm; dramatic

pages.text: He steered as far from the deadly whirlpool as he dared, closer to the monster's rocks, for that was the lesser danger. It was a hard and fearful passage, and it cost him dearly. But the battered ship broke through to open water at last. Odysseus had lost much, yet still he pointed the bow towards Ithaca and would not give up.

image.note: The battered ship emerging from the narrow strait into calm open water, sail torn, Odysseus gripping the tiller and gazing ahead with weary resolve; relief after danger

pages.text: After ten long years of wandering, Odysseus came home to Ithaca at last, alone and disguised as a poor old traveller. His faithful wife Penelope had waited all that time, troubled by rude and greedy men who had taken over his hall. No one knew the ragged stranger, until his old dog lifted its head and knew its master at once.

image.note: A grey-muzzled old dog lifting its head to recognise a ragged, travel-worn Odysseus at the gate of his hall; tender recognition; a tiny ant sits cross-legged on the gatepost nearby, unbothered as ever

pages.text: Odysseus revealed himself, strung the mighty bow that no other man could bend, and drove the troublemakers from his home. Penelope wept with joy, and his son stood tall beside him. The long, hard journey was over. The king was home, the island was at peace, and the family that had waited so faithfully was together once more, and

image.note: Odysseus revealed in his true form, drawing a great bow in his hall, the greedy men fleeing; then Penelope and his son embracing him; joyful reunion, warmth, no visible violence
